body_text:
Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Let $P(z) = a_n z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1 z + a_0$
be a nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients ($a_n \ne 0$ and $n \ge 1$).
Then $P(z)$ has at least one root in $\mathbb{C}$, that is, there exists $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$
such that $P(z_0) = 0$.

Consequently, by polynomial long division and induction on the degree, every degree-$n$
polynomial factors completely into $n$ linear factors:
$$ P(z) = a_n (z - \alpha_1)(z - \alpha_2) \cdots (z - \alpha_n), $$
where $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{C}$ are the roots counted with multiplicity.
In the language of field theory, this theorem establishes that $\mathbb{C}$ is *algebraically closed*,
forming the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{R}$ with $[\mathbb{C} : \mathbb{R}] = 2$.

*Historical and Conceptual Proof Idea*: First claimed by Peter Roth (1608) and Albert Girard (1629),
and partially proved by Jean le Rond d'Alembert (1746), the first rigorous proof was completed
by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1799. Despite its name, every known proof requires topological or
analytic input: the continuous growth of $|P(z)| \to \infty$ as $|z| \to \infty$ forces $|P(z)|$
to attain its global minimum at some point $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$. If $P(z_0) = c \ne 0$, a local
Taylor expansion $P(z_0 + h) = c + b h^k + O(h^{k+1})$ allows choosing $h$ so that $b h^k$ has
direction opposite to $c$, producing a value $|P(z_0 + h)| < |c|$, which contradicts the
minimality of $|P(z_0)|$ (d'Alembert's Lemma). In subsequent sections, we shall witness how
Liouville's Theorem and Cauchy's Residue Theorem yield effortless one-line proofs of this milestone.
